previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: An elderly male with a complex medical history including COPD, CAD s/p CABG, atrial fibrillation, cerebellar degeneration, and prior aspiration pneumonia was admitted for fever and abdominal pain localized to his G-tube site. He reported redness, pain, and drainage around the tube, along with recent cough and nausea. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis, hyponatremia, and a new lung opacity on chest X-ray, prompting concern for pneumonia and G-tube site cellulitis. He was started on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. CT abdomen showed no abscess but confirmed the G-tube in place and extensive diverticulosis. Over the hospital stay, his fever resolved, respiratory status remained stable, and the pneumonia concern was downgraded. He was transitioned to oral Bactrim for cellulitis. The patient expressed a clear desire to have his unused G-tube removed despite risks of aspiration, a decision supported by his healthcare proxy. He was discharged home with services on a 10-day antibiotic course with plans for outpatient G-tube removal, follow-up for iron deficiency anemia, and monitoring of chronic hyponatremia.

the small amount of fluid, lack of concerning signs for 
infection, pulmonology team recommended 1 month follow-up CXR.

symptoms without antibiotics. Pt discharged with lidocaine patch 
for management of MSK pain.

Of note, varicella culture was sent from a possible vesicle at L 
flank, result is pending on day of this note. however, suspicion 
for shingles is low based on lack of skin hypersensitivity, lack 
of neuropathic pain, and lack of dermatomal 
distribution/additional vesicles.

pain, likely related to his atypical chest pain. CTA abd 
obtained given h/o multiple embolic events.  Imaging notable for

FINDINGS:

CT ABDOMEN:

Limited view of lung bases is notable for chronic interstitial changes,
bronchiectasis as well as a small to moderate non-hemorrhagic left pleural
effusion and adjacent collapse versus consolidation.

Liver enhances homogeneously without focal lesions.  There is no intrahepatic
biliary dilatation.  Portal vein is patent.  The gallbladder contains two
calcified stones, as before.  There is no gallbladder wall thickening or
pericholecystic stranding.  The spleen, pancreas and adrenal glands are
unremarkable.  The kidneys contain multiple rounded hypodensities; while the
larger ones are simple cysts, the remaining are too small to characterize.
There is no hydronephrosis.  A small hiatal hernia is noted.  The stomach is
otherwise unremarkable.  Loops of small bowel are normal in course and
caliber.  There is no obstruction.  Colon is notable for extensive
diverticulosis, primarily in the sigmoid without diverticulitis.  There is no
mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  There is no intra-abdominal
free air or fluid.

Bladder, prostate, and seminal vesicles are unremarkable.  There is no pelvic
free fluid or lymphadenopathy.

Severe multilevel degenerative changes are again noted in the imaged spine,
which appear relatively stable compared to the most recent examination.  There
is no concerning osteolytic or osteosclerotic lesion.

CTA:

Moderate atherosclerotic calcification is seen along the abdominal aorta and
its major branches.  Abdominal aorta is of normal caliber without aneurysmal
dilatation.  Calcifications are seen at the ostium of the celiac trunk,
without significant narrowing.  Hepatic arterial anatomy is conventional. 
There is greater than 75% narrowing at the origin of the superior mesenteric
artery.  Calcification are also seen at the ostia of the renal arteries;
however, no high grade stenosis is identified.  The inferior mesenteric artery
is widely patent.  Atherosclerotic disease is also present along the common
iliac arteries and their branches, which remain patent.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Greater than 75% narrowing at the ostium of the superior mesenteric artery
The remaining major branches of the abdominal aorta are widely patent. No
evidence of acute or chronic bowel ischemia.

2.  Diverticulosis without diverticulitis.

3.  Cholelithiasis without cholecystitis.
